meanings.note: polite to one person, or to several people
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'пать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to sleep', paired with 'поспать'.

examples.text: Ладно, утром позвоню ей. Поехали спать.
examples.trans: All right, I'll call her in the morning. Let's go to sleep.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лышать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to hear', forming an aspectual pair with 'услышать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to hear about') (слышать о + prepositional) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Как странно, я ничего об этом не слышал.
examples.trans: How strange, I've heard nothing about it.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('my') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
'дать слово' = to give one's word, 'держать слово' = to keep one's word
'дать слово' = to give one's word, 'держать слово' = to keep one's word

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'a little'.
чуть не + verb: я чуть не упал = I nearly fell

examples.text: Садись, не бойся. Я ведь сам чуть тебя не отпустил.
examples.trans: Sit down, don't be afraid. I very nearly let you go myself.

meanings.note: impersonal, + genitive: денег не хватило = there wasn't enough money
Secondary conversational sense ('that's enough!') (хватит!) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Gum? I didn't have enough money.

examples.text: Хватит спорить из-за пустяков, давайте лучше спокойно работать!
examples.trans: Enough arguing over trifles, let us just work calmly instead!

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'blow, strike' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Удар нужно наносить там, где противник слаб.
examples.trans: You must strike where the enemy is weak.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('your') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'speech' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я должен написать речь для Самсонова.
examples.trans: I must write a speech for Samsonov.

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('fiery, passionate').

examples.text: Твоя утренняя речь перед поварами была очень пламенной.
examples.trans: Your morning speech in front of the cooks was very fiery.

examples.text: Передавай от меня пламенный привет всему вашему коллективу!
examples.trans: Send my warm, passionate regards to your entire team!

говорить.gloss: to speak, to say, to talk

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to speak', forming an aspectual pair with 'сказать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to speak, to talk') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Russian preposition meaning 'from' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('of') (тошнит от = sick of) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: short form чисто: всё чисто = everything is clean
Secondary conversational sense ('pure') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Нин, я всё помыл. Всё чисто.
examples.trans: Nina, I washed everything. It's all clean.

meanings.note: у меня сердце = I have a bad heart (colloquial)

examples.text: Мне горько, мне плохо. У меня сердце.
examples.trans: I feel bitter, I feel awful. I have a bad heart.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: уже четыре года = for four years now

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'second', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'heart attack' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Это уже второй инфаркт за день.
examples.trans: This is already the second heart attack today.

examples.text: От таких новостей у шефа будет второй инфаркт за день.
examples.trans: From news like that, the chef will have a second heart attack today.

examples.text: Врачи сказали, что нужно беречь сердце от инфаркта.
examples.trans: The doctors said that one must protect the heart from a heart attack.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('behind') (+ instrumental) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
на днях = in the next few days, or the other day

examples.trans: I'll call in the next few days.
Any day now, on the website.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'so'.
verb: Что это значит? = What does it mean?
Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.

злиться.gloss: to be angry, to get mad

meanings.en: to be angry, to get mad
meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to be angry', forming an aspectual pair with 'разозлиться'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.text: А знаешь, почему ты так злишься?
examples.trans: And do you know why you are so angry?
Don't be angry with me, please.

examples.text: Хорошо. А знаешь, почему ты так злишься?
examples.trans: Fine. Do you know why you're so angry?

meanings.note: + genitive: 'у нас нет выбора' = we have no choice
Secondary conversational sense ('there isn't') (+ genitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: ничего не осталось = there's nothing left
Secondary conversational sense ('to stay') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to live'.

examples.trans: I live in a communal flat.

examples.text: Я хочу нормально жить! Я хочу биде, понимаешь?
examples.trans: I want to live like a normal person! I want a bidet, do you understand?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'at' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('I have') (possession) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('from (ask from someone)') (просить у кого) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: emphatic at the start of a sentence
Secondary conversational sense ('? = really?, oh yeah?') (disbelief) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.
short form only: рад, рада, радо, рады; no long-form cases

examples.trans: I'm very glad to see you.

examples.text: Ну что ты? Я очень рад тебя видеть.
examples.trans: Oh, come on! I'm very glad to see you.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'now'.

examples.text: Теперь я начальник нашей стройки. Ты уволен!
examples.trans: Now I'm the boss of our building site. You're fired!

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to give', forming an aspectual pair with 'давать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: to take a rest or sleep temporarily

examples.trans: Let us just sleep quietly tonight.
